ranking.rationale: Prior inpatient utilization is one of the most robust predictors of readmission risk and should transfer across domains because it reflects underlying disease burden and recent healthcare use rather than site-specific coding or demographic shortcuts. It offers strong marginal signal at the first step with less brittleness than payer, specialty, race, or medication-pattern features.

Age adds strong, broadly stable signal for readmission risk beyond prior inpatient utilization: older patients generally have higher comorbidity burden, frailty, and care complexity across hospitals and domains. It is less likely than race, payer, specialty, or admission/discharge codes to act as a domain identifier, and less post-treatment/leakage-prone than encounter-management variables or medication changes.

Prior emergency utilization is a strong, semantically stable indicator of future readmission risk and complements inpatient history plus age by capturing a distinct pattern of acute healthcare use. It is less likely than demographics, payer, specialty, or discharge disposition to encode brittle site/domain effects or post-discharge leakage.

Length of stay is a strong, broadly stable marker of illness severity and discharge complexity that complements prior utilization counts without relying on demographics or hospital-specific administrative coding. It is usually predictive of readmission risk across domains and less brittle than payer, specialty, race, or discharge disposition features.

Adds a robust measure of overall comorbidity/clinical complexity that should generalize across domains and complements prior utilization features without relying on demographics, hospital-specific coding, or treatment-pattern artifacts.

Primary diagnosis adds strong, clinically grounded signal about the cause and severity context of the admission beyond utilization counts, age, length of stay, and diagnosis count. It should remain semantically predictive of readmission risk across domains, while being less likely than demographics, payer, specialty, or discharge disposition to act mainly as a domain or hospital-process shortcut.

Adds broadly stable signal about encounter intensity and acute illness burden beyond prior utilization, age, length of stay, diagnosis count, and primary diagnosis. Number of lab procedures is usually predictive of readmission risk across hospitals while being less tied to demographic shortcuts or site-specific administrative coding than race, payer, specialty, or discharge disposition, and less brittle than individual medication-change variables.

Adds strong, broadly stable signal about encounter complexity and treatment intensity beyond labs, diagnoses, utilization, age, and length of stay. It is usually more semantically tied to illness burden/readmission risk than demographics or hospital-specific administrative fields, and is less brittle than payer, specialty, or many medication-specific indicators.

Prior outpatient utilization adds complementary, clinically meaningful history beyond inpatient and emergency counts, capturing chronic care engagement and baseline disease management in a way that should remain predictive across domains. It is less likely than payer, specialty, discharge disposition, or demographics to encode site-specific or shortcut information, and offers broader stable value than sparse medication-specific indicators.

HbA1c result is a clinically central, relatively stable indicator of diabetes control and readmission risk that adds complementary disease-severity information beyond utilization counts, length of stay, diagnoses, labs, and medication count. It is more semantically portable across domains than demographic variables, payer/specialty fields, or many sparse medication-change indicators, while being less likely to encode hospital-specific practice patterns than discharge disposition or admission coding.

Adds complementary, encounter-level severity/treatment intensity signal beyond labs, medications, utilization, and diagnoses already selected. It is generally more semantically tied to illness complexity and care burden than demographic or hospital-specific administrative fields, and is likely to transfer better across domains than payer, specialty, race, gender, or sparse medication-change indicators.

Secondary diagnosis adds substantial stable clinical signal beyond the primary diagnosis and utilization features already selected, capturing comorbidity burden and complication patterns that generalize across domains. It is less likely than demographics, payer, specialty, or discharge disposition to act mainly as a domain identifier, and offers broader marginal value than individual medication-change variables.

Max serum glucose adds clinically meaningful, diabetes-specific severity information that should generalize across domains and complements A1C, diagnoses, utilization, and treatment intensity already selected. It is more stable and less likely to encode site, socioeconomic, or demographic shortcuts than payer, specialty, race, or discharge disposition, while offering broader marginal value than individual medication-change indicators.

Discharge disposition adds strong incremental signal about near-term readmission risk beyond utilization, diagnoses, and labs, capturing post-discharge care setting and illness severity in a way that is generally semantically stable across domains. It is more robust and clinically grounded than demographics, payer, specialty, or many sparse medication-change indicators, while avoiding the stronger domain-specificity of hospital/provider identifiers.

Admission type adds broadly stable clinical acuity/context beyond prior utilization, diagnoses, and length-of-stay features. Emergency/urgent/elective status is semantically linked to readmission risk across domains, while being less likely than payer, specialty, or demographics to act mainly as a domain identifier. It should provide more marginal value than additional medication-change variables, many of which are sparse or redundant with existing severity/treatment features.

Insulin change adds strong clinical signal about diabetes severity and inpatient treatment intensity beyond labs, diagnoses, and utilization already selected. It is more semantically tied to readmission risk than demographic or hospital-process features, and likely more robust across domains than payer, specialty, race, or sparse medication indicators.

Adds complementary comorbidity burden beyond primary/secondary diagnoses and utilization already selected; tertiary diagnosis is clinically meaningful for readmission risk and is more likely to transfer across domains than demographics, payer/provider identifiers, or sparse medication-specific indicators.

Overall diabetes-medication status adds broad, clinically meaningful treatment-intensity information that should remain predictive of readmission across domains. It complements already selected utilization, diagnosis, labs, and insulin features better than sparse drug-specific indicators, while avoiding especially brittle shortcut signals like race, payer, or medical specialty.

Captures whether the treatment regimen was adjusted during the encounter, a clinically meaningful signal of instability and management intensity that should generalize across domains. It adds information beyond insulin and diabetesMed while being less sparse and less domain-specific than individual drug indicators, and avoids relying on demographics or likely hospital/practice-style proxies such as payer_code or medical_specialty.

Metformin adds stable clinical signal about baseline diabetes treatment intensity and outpatient disease management beyond insulin, diabetesMed, and change. It is more semantically tied to readmission risk than demographic or hospital-specific variables, and likely offers broader support and less sparsity than many other medication-specific features.

Adds stable signal about diabetes treatment intensity and regimen choice beyond insulin, metformin, change, and diabetesMed. Glimepiride use is common enough to be informative, reflects underlying disease management rather than site identity, and is less likely than race, gender, payer_code, or medical_specialty to encode demographic shortcuts or domain-specific artifacts.

Glipizide adds likely stable signal about diabetes treatment intensity and regimen choice beyond insulin, metformin, glimepiride, change, and diabetesMed. It is more semantically tied to patient disease management than demographic or hospital-identity features like race, gender, payer_code, or medical_specialty, and should generalize better across domains than sparse rare-drug indicators.

Weight adds clinically meaningful diabetes-severity and treatment-context information that should transfer better across domains than race, gender, payer, specialty, or very rare medication indicators. It is less redundant with the already selected utilization, diagnosis, and common-medication features, and is less likely to act as a domain identifier than administrative variables.

Medical specialty can add clinically meaningful context about case complexity and care pathway beyond diagnoses, utilization, and medications already selected, while being less directly tied to protected demographics than race/gender and typically more informative than very sparse individual drug-change indicators or payer code, which is more domain-specific.

Adds clinically meaningful treatment-intensity information beyond insulin, metformin, glimepiride, and glipizide already selected. Glyburide use/change is a common diabetes-management signal that can reflect disease severity and regimen adjustment linked to readmission risk, while being more semantically stable across domains than race, gender, payer_code, or very rare medication indicators.

Adds treatment-intensity information that is clinically relevant to diabetes severity and management beyond insulin, metformin, sulfonylureas, A1C, and utilization features. It is more likely to transfer across domains than race, gender, payer_code, or very rare medication indicators, while still providing nonredundant signal about medication regimen complexity.

Adds complementary signal about diabetes treatment intensity beyond insulin, metformin, sulfonylureas, pioglitazone, change, and diabetesMed. Rosiglitazone use reflects clinically meaningful glycemic management and comorbidity severity that should transfer across domains, while avoiding the stronger domain/leakage risks of race, gender, and payer_code. It is also likely more informative than the remaining rarer medication indicators.

Sex has modest but generally stable clinical association with diabetes complications and readmission risk, and adds complementary patient-level signal beyond utilization, diagnoses, and treatment features already selected. It is less likely than race or payer_code to act as a domain identifier, and more likely than the remaining rare medication indicators to provide nontrivial marginal value.

Among remaining options, this adds the most plausible stable clinical signal: use/change of another diabetes medication can reflect treatment intensity and glycemic management beyond already selected insulin, metformin, sulfonylureas, change, and diabetesMed. It is less likely than race or payer_code to encode domain or demographic shortcuts, and unlike many other remaining drugs it is not an extremely rare obsolete medication with near-zero marginal value.

Among remaining options, this medication-change feature is the most likely to add small but real clinical signal about diabetes treatment intensity beyond insulin, metformin, sulfonylureas, change, and diabetesMed. It is more semantically tied to patient management than race or payer_code, which are more likely to encode domain or demographic shortcuts, and more useful than the very rare obsolete drug indicators that are often near-constant and brittle across hospitals.

Race can add some residual, semantically relevant risk information for diabetes complications and care patterns beyond utilization, diagnoses, and treatment features already selected. While demographic features can encode shortcuts, it is likely to provide more marginal signal than the remaining mostly rare medication-change indicators, which are sparse, brittle, and largely redundant with existing medication features.

Among remaining options, this medication-change feature is the most plausible to add small but real clinical signal about diabetes treatment intensity beyond insulin, metformin, sulfonylureas, change, and diabetesMed. It is less likely than payer_code to encode domain or socioeconomic shortcuts, and unlike several other remaining drugs it is not essentially near-constant/obsolete to the same degree, so it offers the best marginal stable predictive value.

Among remaining options, this medication-combination feature is the most plausible source of incremental clinical signal about treatment intensity and diabetes severity while being less tied to insurance/domain identity than payer_code. The other remaining drug features are very rare or near-constant in this benchmark, so they are likely to add little stable predictive value beyond the already selected medication and utilization features.

Payer type can add some residual signal about access to care and follow-up, which plausibly affects readmission risk, and it is likely more informative than the remaining medication indicators that are rare, near-constant, or largely redundant with already selected diabetes treatment features. Although payer_code can encode domain and socioeconomic artifacts, the remaining candidates are mostly brittle low-prevalence drug variables with very limited marginal value.

Among the remaining options, this combination-drug feature is the most plausible to add small but real signal about diabetes treatment intensity beyond insulin, metformin, sulfonylureas, change, and diabetesMed. The others are extremely rare, obsolete, or near-constant medications in this dataset, so they are less likely to provide stable marginal value and more likely to reflect sparse hospital-specific prescribing artifacts.

Among the remaining options, this medication-change feature is the most plausible to add small but real signal about diabetes treatment intensity beyond insulin, metformin, sulfonylureas, change, and diabetesMed. The other candidates are mostly extremely rare, obsolete, withdrawn, or near-constant drugs that are less likely to contribute stable predictive value and more likely to add sparsity or site-specific prescribing artifacts.

Among the remaining options, this combination therapy indicator is the most plausible to add small but real signal about diabetes severity and treatment intensity beyond already selected single-drug features. The other candidates are mostly extremely rare, obsolete, or near-constant medications in this dataset, making them less useful and less stable for OOD generalization.

Among the remaining options, this adds the most plausible incremental clinical signal while being less likely than others to be a pure rarity artifact. It captures treatment intensity/adjustment information related to glycemic management that can remain predictive across domains, whereas most other candidates are extremely rare or obsolete medications/combinations with near-zero stable value and higher risk of encoding hospital-specific prescribing patterns.

Among the remaining options, this combination-drug feature is the least likely to be entirely constant and can still add a small amount of clinically meaningful treatment-intensity information beyond insulin, diabetesMed, change, and single-drug indicators. The other candidates are mostly extremely rare, obsolete, or near-constant medications in this benchmark, making them even more brittle and lower-value for stable OOD generalization.

Among the remaining options, this rare sulfonylurea medication signal is the most plausible to add small but genuine clinical information about diabetes treatment intensity/history beyond already selected meds. The others are largely near-constant or obsolete drugs in this dataset, making them even more likely to contribute only noise or site-specific prescribing artifacts.

Among the remaining options, this rare medication-change feature is the least obviously obsolete or near-constant and can add a small amount of treatment-intensity information beyond insulin, metformin, sulfonylureas, and change/diabetesMed. The others are largely extremely sparse discontinued drugs or combination therapies with even lower expected marginal value, so this is the best remaining stable signal despite being weak.

Among the remaining options, this combination-therapy indicator is the only one with plausible nonzero variation and some residual clinical signal about treatment intensity after accounting for insulin, diabetesMed, change, and major single-drug features. The others are extremely rare or effectively constant in the diabetes_readmission benchmark, so they add little stable predictive value.

Among the remaining medication indicators, this one is the least likely to act as a demographic or site shortcut and is at least a direct treatment-status variable tied to diabetes management. The other candidates are similarly rare/near-constant, so marginal value is very small overall; this is effectively a weak tie-break among low-information drug features.

Among the remaining options, this medication feature is the least implausible to add any residual signal, though likely very small. Troglitazone and citoglipton are especially rare/obsolete and mostly encode sparse prescribing artifacts, while acetohexamide may capture a tiny amount of treatment-intensity information that is marginally more stable across domains.

Troglitazone is the slightly better final choice because, while both remaining medication features are extremely rare and likely add little beyond the many diabetes-treatment variables already selected, troglitazone has at least some plausible signal as an indicator of intensive or atypical diabetes management. Citoglipton is effectively absent in this dataset and is even less likely to provide stable marginal predictive value.

Only remaining candidate. Its marginal stable value is extremely low because citoglipton is essentially never used in this dataset and is likely near-constant, adding little beyond the many medication indicators already selected.
